consensus_summary: Tares symbolize the wicked—“children of the evil one”—sown by the devil among the righteous and left until separation and destruction at the final judgment. They are often applied more specifically to counterfeit or hypocritical believers.
book_summary: Tares are the enemy-sown counterfeit among the wheat: children of the wicked one who mimic the true grain until harvest, when they are bundled and burned. The entry distinguishes them from chaff.
consensus_core_identification: Tares = wicked people, explicitly the children of the evil one, among the righteous until final judgment.
book_core_identification: Tares = counterfeit people among the wheat, explicitly the children of the wicked one, destined for burning at harvest.
boundary_disagreement: None material. The book foregrounds the counterfeit quality and distinguishes tares from chaff, but neither point excludes or adds cases relative to the consensus core.
material_contradiction: None. Both identify the tares with the children of the wicked one rather than with doctrine, impersonal evil, or chaff.
rationale: After reducing both readings to their minimum identification, they are the same: tares are the wicked children of the evil one placed among the righteous until eschatological separation. The book’s language about mimicking wheat is a botanical and interpretive elaboration already represented in the consensus, while its distinction from winnowed chaff clarifies a neighboring symbol without changing the referent.
strongest_objection: The phrase “counterfeit sown among the wheat” could be read as narrowing the referent to false believers within the visible church, whereas Matthew 13:38 says the field is the world and the consensus permits wicked people more broadly. However, the book immediately uses the text’s broad identification, “children of the wicked one,” so no material narrowing is established.
